strengths: Well-motivated practical problem addressing real deployment challenges (guard-model overhead); elegant solution of reusing serving LLM computation
Comprehensive multi-backbone evaluation across three architectures (Llama-3.2-3B, GPT-OSS-20B, Qwen3-30B-A3B) demonstrates architectural generalization with consistent method ranking

Strong empirical results with favorable parameter efficiency tradeoffs (35M vs 7-8B parameters) achieving competitive or exceeding performance on safety benchmarks (ToxicChat: 84.51 F1; WildGuardMix: 88.55 F1)
Systematic experimental design with ~100 hyperparameter configurations per dataset, clear in-distribution and OOD evaluation, and proper ablations (Table 7: downcasting sensitivity)
Interpretability analysis (Figures 2, 4) provides evidence that task-relevant signals are distributed across layers, supporting learned aggregation over fixed readouts
Practical efficiency gains: 2× speedup over smallest guard baseline with preserved single-model serving footprint (Table 5); maintains near-serving latency
Clean two-stage aggregation architecture with three instantiations showing clear expressiveness-parameter tradeoff; uniform treatment of both stages enables controlled comparisons
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: core contribution applies standard techniques (pooling, learned attention gates, downcast MHA) to probe aggregation; similar multi-layer fusion explored in related work (EAGLE-3)

Concerning out-of-distribution performance for safety applications: substantial drops when training on WildGuardMix→testing ToxicChat (scoring attention −19.6%, MHA −13.9%); direct pooling catastrophically degrades (−27.2%); critical flaw for evolving threat landscapes
Asymmetric cross-architecture evaluation: safety benchmarks evaluated on all three backbones, but sentiment/emotion tasks only on Llama-3.2-3B, limiting confidence in NLU generalization claims
High hyperparameter sensitivity for simpler methods: Pooling and Scoring Attention show extreme variance (PR-AUC 0.2–0.9 range) across learning rates (Figure 3); fragility not adequately addressed

Safety-critical limitations inadequately treated: classification-only (no contextual refusals), silent failures on novel harm categories, requires full retraining for new threats, cannot adapt to evolving attacks

Incomplete evaluation on realistic scenarios: latency benchmarks use max_new_tokens=1 and batch size 1; sequence length constraints acknowledged but not empirically evaluated; real deployments use longer sequences
Downcasting factor requires per-dataset tuning (32 for ToxicChat vs. 8 for SST-2), undermining generality and parameter-efficiency claims; unclear how to select for new tasks
Limited baseline coverage: MULI is only logit-reuse baseline; ShieldHead comparison limited; WildGuard (88.9 F1) substantially outperforms MHA (88.55 F1), narrowing claimed advantages
Bias and fairness not evaluated despite acknowledged risks of inheriting frozen backbone biases; no demographic performance analysis (particularly concerning for safety moderation)
Limited error analysis: observations that errors follow predicted-class patterns lack deeper investigation; no systematic analysis of failure modes by prompt type

strengths: Well-motivated practical problem: addresses genuine production system challenges (orchestration cost, latency, memory) with clear relevance to practitioners
Principled BERTology foundation: effectively leverages established findings that task-relevant features distribute across layers; sensible shift from 'can we reuse?' to 'where should we read out?'

Comprehensive experimental evaluation within scope: multiple benchmarks (ToxicChat, WildGuardMix, IMDB, SST-2, Emotion), proper train/val/test splits, ~100 hyperparameter configurations per dataset, uncertainty quantification, cross-dataset generalization testing

Strong interpretability analysis: Section 5 layer attention visualizations (Figures 2, 4) provide clear empirical evidence that different classes rely on different layer distributions, validating core hypothesis
Significant parameter efficiency: 35M parameters for MHA probe achieves 84.51 F1 on ToxicChat vs. 780M+ for standalone classifiers and billions for guard models
System-level benchmarking: Table 5 effectively demonstrates single-pass reuse preserves memory/latency profiles compared to guard→serve pipelines, making practical case compelling
High reproducibility: code promised, hyperparameters fully documented, search ranges detailed, standard benchmarks used
weaknesses: Critical scope limitation—single model only: Evaluated exclusively on Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct despite title emphasizing 'LLM Orchestrations' (plural), suggesting generality. Claim that 'stronger backbones offer natural path to improved accuracy' is hypothesis, not validated. Different model families (GPT, Gemma, Mistral) and sizes (1B-70B+) may encode task-relevant information differently across layers; generalization to other backbones remains completely unexplored

Limited technical novelty: Two-stage aggregation is straightforward; scoring attention and MHA are standard techniques. No empirical justification for using identical aggregation for both stages. Missing ablations: two-stage vs. single-stage, shared vs. per-layer gates, alternative token-layer fusion schemes

Cross-dataset OOD comparison concerns: Table 2 mixes heterogeneous baselines (different architectures, training data); results presented as competitive despite acknowledged limitations. Single WildGuardMix→ToxicChat transfer trajectory insufficient for generalization claims

Incomplete architectural exploration: No comparison to single-layer learned selection; no ablation of two-stage design; Stage 1 uses L independent gates without justification or ablation of alternatives

Fairness evaluation absent: Ethical considerations mention bias/disparate impact but provide zero empirical evaluation; critical for safety applications like toxicity detection. No demographic breakdown or error rate analysis across subgroups
Limited task scope: Only single-label classification tested; no token-level tasks (NER), multi-label classification, or longer-form documents (acknowledged VRAM constraints limit to ~512 tokens)
Minimum data requirements unclear: Smallest dataset SST-2 (7K examples); no evaluation with <5K or >100K examples to characterize learning curves, especially for parameter-intensive MHA variant

Shallow error analysis: Section 5 observations about misclassification patterns (e.g., layer weights aligning with predicted class) are descriptive but not deeply investigated. Why atypical representations occur remains unexplored

Statistical rigor gaps: Reported mean ± std but no significance tests; some differences approach variance margins (e.g., Emotion 84.58 vs. 87.68 ± 1.09); no statistical validation of attention profile differences (Figure 2, 4)

Baseline comparison gaps: SentriLlama (strong comparable) receives minimal analysis despite similar frozen-backbone philosophy; limited engagement with probing literature; MULI baseline details sparse
